title: The hypertrophy series: strength baseline control for recovery & gains
summary: Introduces the 'baseline': your ability to reproduce the same performance (same weight, same reps) after exertion. It exists between sessions (recovery, which dictates frequency and heavy/light days) and within a session. Quality sets are those that break your ability to return to baseline within the workout; sets you can repeat endlessly (e.g. easy push-ups, 5x5 with equal reps across sets) accumulate lower-quality tonnage, except in nucleus overload where repeatability is the point.

claims.claim: The 'baseline' is your ability to reproduce an effort: e.g. how long it takes after a set of 10 squats before you can again do 10 reps with the same weight.
You must know and control every training variable; if you don't control them, they control you.
Baseline exists in two dimensions: within a workout (between sets) and between workouts (recovery).
For a bodybuilder, the program is determined by recovery: attack the muscle as hard and as often as possible, damage it, recover enough to repeat the cycle and progress.
Growth is a virtuous circle: a bigger muscle has more fibers to break, so it can take more damage and tonnage, which makes it grow more.

Between-session baseline dictates frequency and heavy vs light days: after a heavy Monday squat you might do quad accessories Wednesday without pushing them, because strength may not be back to baseline even if the quads have mostly recovered.
Within-workout baseline is the most important variable to control for pushing tonnage and progression, because it defines which sets are hard, beneficial sets.
The more taxing a set, the longer it takes to return to baseline; a true 1RM deadlift cannot be repeated in the same session no matter how long you rest, and may take days to recover.

At the other extreme, sets that are too easy barely register as fatigue; push-ups for an advanced, not heavy bencher can be repeated almost forever, so they are poor for building big muscles despite accumulating tonnage.
You want lifts that prevent you from returning to baseline, because that means you are digging into the fibers enough that they need a break, recover and grow.
Sets that challenge your ability to return to baseline are quality sets, i.e. 'hard sets'.
In a 5x5 where you get 5 reps on the first and last set, the first set didn't challenge your baseline; evolving rep ranges are better suited to dig deeper.
Nucleus overload is the exception: its movements should never cause fatigue that prevents repeating the feat, since its whole concept is repeatability to accumulate volume.
Outside nucleus overload, train so that if you redo a set after 3 minutes of rest you can't get as many reps.
Structure the workout by starting with working sets and strength work, then pyramid down through variations and accessories so that by the end your ability to return to baseline is shot.
At the start of his bench session he can do 50 push-ups repeatedly; at the end he gets about 30, then 25, then 20, which shows the muscles can no longer recover within the workout, which is the goal.
Every lift should be hard enough that the muscle needs days to adapt, not just the 3-4 minutes of rest between sets; that signals enough damage to grow.
Not all tonnage is equal; junk volume exists. Volume that never challenged your baseline isn't worthless but is worse because it doesn't promote progression, and you accumulate less than you think.

exercises.name: Push-ups
cues: do them at the end of a bench session when fatigued
exercises.why: fresh they are too easy for an advanced lifter to challenge baseline; fatigued they become quality sets
